title: Fallback + Tiered Spillover Architecture notes
content:
Summary:
A concise runbook-style design for graceful degradation across model variants, tiered capacity buckets, and regional spillover. Goal: keep customer-facing requests successful (200-level) and as useful as possible while protecting latency SLOs and avoiding cost blowouts.

Goals:
- Ensure >99% success (non-error) for hosted API during partial capacity loss.
- Keep P50 latency within SLOs for premium routes; offer degraded-but-acceptable responses for best-effort routes.
- Respect data residency and customer routing constraints.
- Make fallbacks deterministic, observable, and reversible.

Assumptions:
- We have 3 model variants per family: full (fp16/float), quantized (int8/4), distilled (smaller architecture).
- Capacity tiers: reserved (dedicated pools), burst (short-term shared capacity), best-effort (low-priority preemptible).
- Regions are organized in rings: primary region -> neighboring region(s) -> global fallback region.
- Control plane can evaluate policy metadata on each request (customer tier, model family, region preference, data residency).

High-level routing flows (pseudo):
1) Receive request with route tags (customer_tier, region_pref, model_family).
2) Check circuit-breaker state per model_family+region.
3) Try reserved pool in preferred region (full model).
4) If unavailable or queueing predicted >latency_slo: attempt burst pool (same region) with same model.
5) If burst unavailable or cost threshold exceeded: degrade to quantized variant in reserved pool.
6) If still cannot meet latency target: spillover to neighboring region reserved pool (respect data_residency flag).
7) Final fallback: distilled variant in best-effort pool OR cached response if strong prefix match.
8) If request is marked non-essential (telemetry/test), fail fast with a 429/503 and brief explanatory payload.

Degradation modes (ordered by preference to preserve quality):
- Transparent model variant swap (full -> quantized) with identical API signature.
- Disable streaming to reduce tail latency and CPU overhead; return batched full response.
- Reduce max tokens / enforce earlier end-of-sequence heuristics.
- Route to distilled model offering shorter context and lower quality.
- Serve cached or precomputed answer when applicable (prefix cache / reranker fallback).

Decision matrix (example policies):
- Tier: enterprise/reserved: allow cross-region spillover but only to regions with contractual residency match; try full->quantized before cross-region.
- Tier: self-serve/dev: prefer degraded model locally; only spill to other regions if explicit opt-in.
- Model-critical endpoints (e.g., moderation): fail open? No — prefer distilled/more conservative model; critical safety paths must never route to best-effort.

Control plane responsibilities:
- Central policy engine that evaluates per-request priority, allowed fallbacks, and cost caps.
- Maintain live capacity map: per-region, per-model-variant available slots and queue depth predictions.
- Emit real-time signals to serving runtime: throttle directives, circuit-breaker toggles, and routing hints.
- Expose debug endpoints for on-call to trigger manual failover/rollback.

Operational signals to monitor:
- Model variant swap rate (spikes indicate sustained pressure).
- Spillover frequency and average added latency per spill.
- Cache hit ratio for prefix/KV cache used as fallback.
- Cost delta when using cross-region vs local degraded variants.
- Error rates by degradation mode (e.g., distilled quality regression alerts).
- Customer-impact traces: per-customer SLO, degraded-response counts.

Safety, privacy, and compliance:
- Data residency flag must be enforced in control-plane decisions; cross-region only if allowed.
- Audit logs for every forced spillover/fallback event (who/what triggered it).
- Encryption and key handling unchanged when routing across regions; ensure KMS access is available in fallback region.

Implementation plan (MVP):
- Phase 0: policy DSL prototype + unit tests (1 sprint). DSL expresses allowed fallbacks per customer-tier and model-family.
- Phase 1: basic routing changes in control plane: prefer quantized variant before cross-region (2 sprints).
- Phase 2: integrate capacity map and queue prediction model; add metrics and alerting (3 sprints).
- Phase 3: gradual rollout via canary routes; enable manual rollback hooks and SRE runbook (2 sprints).

Back-of-envelope cost notes:
- Quantized inference reduces GPU throughput cost ~1.7–2.5x depending on perf.
- Cross-region egress + KMS may add 15–40% per request in cost; prefer local degraded variant for cost control.

Open questions / TBDs:
- How to declaratively represent multi-step fallbacks in the policy DSL (linear vs tree-shaped)?
- Should we surface a degraded flag in the API response so customers can A/B their UX? (pros: transparency; cons: blobs in logs)
- How to handle long-running streaming sessions that cross a fallback boundary mid-stream? (option: terminate+restart on new variant)
- Rollout signals: what percentile increase in swap rate triggers auto-escalation to SRE?

Next steps / actions:
- Sync with serving-runtime (Ravi) on cost/latency tradeoffs of quantized vs distilled on V100/A100/TPUs.
- Prototype a small policy DSL fragment and add it to GH draft PR (ref: GH:github.com/redwood/infra/pull/789).
- Add ENG-3456 to propose SLO changes for degraded responses and add a customer-facing note for opt-in behavior.

Notes to self:
- Keep fallback decisions simple and deterministic for first rollout.
- Avoid too many simultaneous fallbacks; prefer one graceful degradation per request at a time.
- Document edge-cases in on-call runbook: KMS outage, entire-region outage, mass spillover.

References:
- Linked artifacts above for implementation context (ENG-3456, GH PR).
- See Slack thread #platform-routing for recent outage play-by-play.
